## Task input
## Task: Inject TimeProvider into product-side retry delays

Replace every `Task.Delay(delay, cancellationToken)` in the production source code that lacks a `TimeProvider` argument with `Task.Delay(delay, timeProvider ?? TimeProvider.System, cancellationToken)` and thread the `TimeProvider?` parameter through to the call site. This lets test suites drive those delays with `ManualTimeProvider` instead of real wall-clock seconds.

### Baseline measurements

From `llm-tasks/completed/speed-up-automated-tests/timings-baseline.txt`, the full suite runs at ~119 s wall time. The product-side delays below are real-time `Task.Delay` calls that tests exercise but cannot currently accelerate:

| Location | Delay | Purpose | Real cost per hit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `src/VisualRelay.Core/Execution/BackendLifecycle.Start.cs:172` | 1 000 ms | startup readiness polling | 1 s per startup iteration |
| `src/VisualRelay.Core/Execution/BackendLifecycle.cs:147` | 200 ms | stop‑sequence yield | 200 ms per stop |
| `src/VisualRelay.Core/Execution/PlanningWorktree.cs:224` | 250 ms‑1 s | git‑op retry backoff | 250 ms – 1 s per retry |
| `src/VisualRelay.Core/Execution/PlanningWorktree.cs:232` | 250 ms‑1 s | git‑op retry backoff | 250 ms – 1 s per retry |
| `src/VisualRelay.Core/Execution/GitCommitter.cs:250` | 250 ms‑1 s | git‑op retry backoff | 250 ms – 1 s per retry |

None of these accept a `TimeProvider` — they burn real seconds under any test that enters a retry or polling path.

### Prescribed approach

1. Follow the established pattern in the codebase (see `ProcessRunners.cs:64`, `SandboxedTestRunner.Watched.cs:88`, `ProcessCapture.cs:73`, `ProcessRunners.Watchdog.cs:78`): add a `TimeProvider? timeProvider = null` parameter to each method, sinking to `TimeProvider.System` at the call site.

2. Replace:
   ```csharp
   await Task.Delay(delay, cancellationToken);
   ```
   with:
   ```csharp
   await Task.Delay(delay, tp, cancellationToken);
   ```
   where `tp = timeProvider ?? TimeProvider.System`.

3. Thread the parameter through intermediate methods so the test call site can inject a `ManualTimeProvider`.

4. In tests that exercise a retry or poll path, inject a `ManualTimeProvider` and use the Advance-loop pattern established in `BackendReadinessProbeTests.cs`:
   ```csharp
   var time = new ManualTimeProvider();
   var task = MethodUnderTest(..., timeProvider: time);
   while (!task.IsCompleted)
   {
       time.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(delayMs));
       await Task.Yield();
   }
   var result = await task;
   ```

5. Keep a small set of integration tests (tagged with `SlowIntegration.SkipIfNotOptedIn()`) that exercise the real-time path with `TimeProvider.System` to retain confidence that wall-clock delays work in production.

### Expected saving (estimate — verify by measurement)

- **BackendLifecycle tests**: ~1 s saved per startup‑retry scenario, ~200 ms per stop.
- **GitCommitter/PlanningWorktree tests**: ~250 ms – 1 s per retry scenario.
- Estimated total: ~2–3 s of full‑suite wall time. This is an estimate, not a measurement — the real numbers come from timing the suite before and after, per the commit-message evidence section below. More importantly, this removes an entire class of hidden wall-clock waste from tests that trigger error-recovery paths.

### Pitfalls

- Do NOT delete the delay itself — the backoff is intentional (prevents busy‑retry hammering).
- Every `Task.Delay` that gets a TimeProvider must keep its `CancellationToken`.
- `RealSleepGuardTests` scans the **test project only** — it will not flag these product-side delays, before or after. Verify the product change directly instead: grep the five sites listed above and confirm every `Task.Delay` there passes a TimeProvider. The test-side guard must simply stay green.

### Coverage rules

- Never delete, disable, skip, or weaken a test. Speed comes from doing the same verification cheaper, not from verifying less.
- Any test that genuinely requires a real-time boundary should use `SlowIntegration.SkipIfNotOptedIn()` and run only with `VR_RUN_SLOW_INTEGRATION=1`. The default suite covers the same logic with virtual time.

### Commit‑message evidence

Measure the full-suite wall time right before starting and right after finishing.
Then put exactly one filled-in evidence bullet in the commit message body, following
the attached `commit-message-evidence.md`. Do not write the numbers into this task
file — real measured numbers belong in the commit message only.

**Task framing**

The production build contains five `Task.Delay` calls across three classes (`BackendLifecycle`, `PlanningWorktree`, `GitCommitter`) that serve intentional backoff/polling purposes (readiness polling, stop-sequence yield, git-op retries). None accept a `TimeProvider`, so any test that triggers these paths burns real wall-clock seconds. The codebase already has an established pattern — `ProcessRunners.cs`, `ProcessCapture.cs`, `SandboxedTestRunner.Watched.cs`, `ProcessRunners.Watchdog.cs` — where `TimeProvider? timeProvider = null` is threaded through as an optional parameter and sunk to `TimeProvider.System` at the call site. The task is to apply that same pattern to the five product-side delays so that tests can inject a `ManualTimeProvider` and advance virtual time instantly instead of waiting.

---

### Option A — Per‑method injection (prescribed, matches existing pattern)

In each of the five locations, add `TimeProvider? timeProvider = null` to the enclosing method, resolve `var tp = timeProvider ?? TimeProvider.System` once, and switch each `Task.Delay(delay, ct)` to `Task.Delay(delay, tp, ct)`. Thread the parameter through any intermediate method that sits between the public API and the delay.

- **Pros**: Follows the exact pattern already established in four other files — consistent, reviewable, low surprise. Test call sites can opt in with zero change to existing callers (default stays `null` → `TimeProvider.System`). Minimal diff per location.
- **Cons**: Threads a `TimeProvider?` parameter through every method that contains or passes through a delay, even when most callers never pass a custom provider. Five independent edits, each needing its own test update. Does not help any *future* delay that might be added without this parameter.

---

### Option B — Constructor‑level TimeProvider field

Add an `IReadOnlyList<TimeProvider>` or singular `TimeProvider` property to each class (`BackendLifecycle`, `PlanningWorktree`, `GitCommitter`), initialized from the constructor (defaulting to `TimeProvider.System`). The delay sites read `this._timeProvider` instead of a method parameter.

- **Pros**: Cleaner method signatures — no threading through every intermediate call. A single injection point per class makes it easy for a test constructor/factory to set the provider once. Scales better if more delays are added to the same class later.
- **Cons**: Requires constructor changes in three classes (or their factory/DI setup), which may ripple to other consumers. If the class is constructed in many places, each needs a new optional parameter or overload. The existing codebase pattern (Option A) is per‑method, so this would introduce a second, different convention.

---

### Option C — Extract retry‑backoff helper with its own TimeProvider

Pull the exponential‑backoff delay pattern (shared by `PlanningWorktree` and `GitCommitter`) into a dedicated helper — say `RetryBackoff` — that owns a `TimeProvider` field and exposes an `async Task WaitAsync(TimeSpan delay, CancellationToken ct)`. Instantiate the helper once per retry loop, passing `TimeProvider?` at construction.

- **Pros**: Eliminates duplication across `PlanningWorktree` and `GitCommitter` (both use 250 ms–1 s backoff). A single tested helper means one place to verify, one place to inject `ManualTimeProvider`. Aligns with the DRY principle and makes the retry policy itself unit‑testable in isolation.
- **Cons**: Larger refactor — requires extracting the backoff logic, understanding the exact retry semantics at each site, and replacing inline `Task.Delay` + loop code with the helper. The `BackendLifecycle` delays (readiness polling, stop yield) are different patterns and wouldn't benefit from the same helper, so they'd still need Option A. Higher risk of behavioural drift during extraction.
